ab.note: “a” before consonants; “ab” before vowels and h (and at times before consonants too: ab hómine).

absolutio.note: A noun from absólvere — to loose, to set free; absolution looses from guilt.

adiutorium.note: A noun from adjuváre — to help.

aeternus.note: Contracted from ævitérnus, from ævum — an age, a long span of time.

affligo.note: Literally to dash against the ground (ad + fligo); hence to afflict.

agnus.note: “Ecce Agnus Dei” (Jn 1:29) — the Baptist's words at the Jordan; hence the Lamb as a liturgical name of Christ.

ago.note: A verb of very broad meaning; in the liturgy most often in the idiom “grátias ágere” — to give thanks.

altare.note: Classical Latin calls an altar ara; altáre (more often the plural altária) is the word of Scripture and the liturgy.

altus.note: The superlative “Altíssimus” — the Most High — is a constant scriptural title of God.

amen.note: A Hebrew word taken into Latin unchanged — indeclinable; the solemn seal of a prayer.

anima.note: The same root as ánimus (mind, spirit); ánima is the breath that gives life.

apostolicus.note: The adjective of apóstolus (apostle) — coming from the Apostles, belonging to them.

ascendo.note: A compound of ad (toward) + scándere (to climb) — the exact opposite of descéndere.

aufero.note: A compound of ab + fero — to carry off; it inflects irregularly, like fero. Its supine ablátum gave the ablative case its name.

aveo.note: A defective verb: in practice almost only the imperatives “ave”, “avéte”, used as a greeting.

baptisma.note: A Greek loanword (báptisma — an immersion), neuter, declined in the 3rd declension: genitive baptísmatis.

Baptista.note: A 1st-declension noun, yet masculine — like “agrícola”, farmer; from Greek “baptistés” — one who immerses.

benedico.note: A compound of bene (well) + dícere (to say) — to bless is literally “to speak well”.

benedictus.note: From “bene dícere” — to speak well (of someone).

caelum.note: The plural “cæli” is masculine; biblical Latin often speaks of heaven in the plural, after the Hebrew idiom.

catholicus.note: From Greek katholikós — universal, taken as a whole.

Christus.note: Greek Christós — “the anointed one” — rendering Hebrew Mashiach (Messiah).

cithara.note: The Greek κιθάρα; in the psalms a stringed instrument sung to.

clamor.note: A noun from clamáre — to cry out; in the psalms the cry is prayer.

confiteor.note: In church Latin also “to praise”: Confitémini Dómino.

conglorifico.note: A rare compound of cum (together) + glorificáre; it calques a Greek verb built with syn- (together with).

consubstantialis.note: A theological coinage rendering Greek homooúsios — of the same substance; formed from cum + substántia.

conturbo.note: A compound of cum + turbáre — to stir up thoroughly.

converto.note: A compound of cum + vértere — to turn; the passive often means to turn oneself toward someone.

credo.note: Classically with the dative of the person (credo tibi — I believe you); the profession of faith says “credo in” with the accusative — I believe in. The whole Symbol of faith is named the Credo after its first word.

crucifigo.note: A running-together of cruci fígere — to fasten to a cross (crux, crucis + fígere).

de.note: Close to ex, but ex points to coming out from inside, de to separation from something or motion downward.

descendo.note: A compound of de (down) + scándere (to climb).

deus.note: Classical Latin avoided a vocative of “deus”; Church Latin simply calls “Deus”.

dextera.note: Understand “(manus) déxtera” — the right hand; “at the right hand” is Scripture's place of honor.

dies.note: One of the few 5th-declension nouns; usually masculine, feminine especially of an appointed day.

dignor.note: A deponent (passive form, active meaning) from dignus — worthy; dignéris is a courteous petition: be pleased to.

discerno.note: A compound of dis + cérnere — to separate, to sift apart.

dono.note: From “donum”, a gift. It gives a thing (accusative) to a person (dative); classical Latin can also reverse the pattern and present a person (accusative) with something (ablative).

ecclesia.note: From Greek ekklesía — an assembly of those called out; Christian Latin uses it both of the community and of the building.

eleison.note: Greek ἐλέησον, the imperative of ἐλεέω “to have mercy”. In Greek it is an aorist: mercy asked for as a single act. Like Kýrie, the word has no entry of its own in the Latin dictionaries.

eruo.note: Literally to dig out; hence to snatch someone from danger.

ex.note: Before a vowel always “ex”; before a consonant both “e” and “ex” occur (ex María Vírgine).

exaudio.note: An intensified audíre — not merely to hear but to grant what is heard.

excelsus.note: “In excélsis” — in the highest, that is, in the heavens; the plural follows the Hebrew idiom of the psalms.

exspecto.note: A compound of ex + spectáre (to look) — to look out for; some editions print the simplified spelling “expécto”.

facio.note: In the present system its passive is supplied by fio (to become); the perfect passive is factus sum.

factor.note: A noun from fácere (to make) — “the one who makes”; in the Creed a title of God as maker of all.

finis.note: In the plural fines means boundaries, and hence the territory they enclose.

fio.note: Irregular; serves as the passive of “fácere”, to do or make.

fortitudo.note: From fortis — strong; in the psalms God's might, among the virtues fortitude.

gens.note: The same root as gígnere — to beget; a gens is those sprung from one stock.

gigno.note: The present stem is reduplicated (gi-gn-o) beside the root gen- seen in génui and génitum.

hic.note: The adverb of place; not the demonstrative hic, hæc, hoc — this.

hosanna.note: A Hebrew cry, “save, we pray”, from Ps 117:25; on the lips of the crowd greeting Christ (Mt 21:9) it is already pure acclamation — which is why Latin leaves it untranslated. Indeclinable.

Iesus.note: The Greek form of Hebrew Yeshua — “the Lord saves”; irregular declension (nominative Jesus, accusative Jesum, all other cases Jesu).

ille.note: The demonstrative of what is farther off; in Christian Latin often simply he. The Romance definite articles (il, le, el) descend from it.

incarno.note: A verb of Christian Latin, formed from caro, carnis (flesh).

incedo.note: A compound of in + cédere — to step forward; it names a manner of walking, not motion in general.

indulgentia.note: In the Church's language it became a technical term: an indulgence, the remission of temporal punishment.

indulgeo.note: It governs the dative of the person: indulgére alicui — to be gracious to someone.

inimicus.note: The negation of amícus (friend): in- + amícus.

iniquitas.note: From iníquus; at the bottom of it lies the lack of æquus — of what is even and fair.

iniquus.note: The negation of æquus (even, fair): in- + æquus.

introeo.note: A compound of intro (inwards) + ire (to go); it inflects irregularly, like ire. Its supine gives intróitus — an entrance, and hence the name of the entrance chant.

invisibilis.note: The negation of visíbilis by the prefix in-.

ipse.note: The intensive pronoun: it presses on the person or thing spoken of.

iudico.note: Formed from júdex (judge), itself from jus, juris (law) + dícere (to speak) — the one who declares the law.

iuventus.note: From júvenis — young; the collective noun also means the young as a body.

kyrie.note: Greek κύριε, the vocative of κύριος “lord”. No Latin dictionary heads the bare word — Latin took the whole formula instead: Niermeyer heads kyrie-eleison as a noun for the chant itself, and Du Cange has kyrieles for the litany and the verb kyrieleisare, “to sing Kyrie eleison”.

laetifico.note: A compound of lætus (glad) + fácere — to make glad.

laetor.note: A deponent (passive form, active meaning) from lætus — glad.

loquor.note: It stresses speaking as an activity; dícere stresses what is said.

lumen.note: The same root as lux; lumen is usually light as it is seen — brightness, or a lamp.

lux.note: Lux is light itself; lumen is the light a thing gives off (compare lumen de lúmine in the Credo).

mereor.note: A deponent (passive form, active meaning); mereámur — that we may be counted worthy.

meritum.note: The noun of meréri — to deserve.

Michael.note: From Hebrew Mika'el — “Who is like God?”.

misereor.note: In liturgical formulas with the dative (miserére nobis); classically and in the psalms with the genitive (miserére mei).

misericordia.note: A compound of míserum cor — a heart for the wretched; the same build as miséricors.

misericors.note: A compound of miser (wretched) + cor (heart): having a heart for the wretched.

mortuus.note: The perfect participle of mórior (to die), used both as an adjective and as a noun: mórtui, the dead.

nascor.note: From the participle natus come natúra and natívitas (nativity).

non.note: It negates a single word or a whole clause; prohibitions and negative petitions use ne instead.

oratio.note: The noun of oráre; in classical Latin a speech, in Christian Latin chiefly a prayer.

oro.note: The call “Orémus” — let us pray — is the same verb.

ostendo.note: A compound of obs (ob) + téndere — to stretch out before someone.

patior.note: From the participle passus comes pássio — suffering, the Passion.

peccatum.note: The noun of pecco (to sin) — the deed, not the disposition.

per.note: It expresses mediation — hence the standing close of the orations, “per Christum Dóminum nostrum”.

senses: to bring all the way to
perduco.note: A compound of per + dúcere — to lead right to the end.

Pilatus.note: A Roman cognomen; Pilate governed Judea for Rome under the emperor Tiberius.

plebs.note: At Rome the order set against the patricians; in Church Latin simply the people.

senses: full of (with the ablative or genitive)

Pontius.note: A Roman clan name (nomen); Pilátus was the cognomen that went with it.

senses: to proceed, to come forth from
procedo.note: A compound of pro (forward) + cédere (to go); in trinitarian language it is the verb for one divine Person's origin from another.

propheta.note: A 1st-declension noun, yet masculine — like “agrícola”, farmer; from Greek “prophétes” — one who speaks for another.

quaeso.note: A defective verb: chiefly quæso and quǽsumus survive, dropped into a request as English drops in “please”. It is an older form of the verb quærere — to seek, to ask for.

quare.note: A fusion of qua re — for what cause.

quia.note: Classical Latin mostly “because”; church Latin, following the Greek, also uses “quia” for “that” after verbs of saying and confessing.

quotidianus.note: In the Lord's Prayer it renders the Greek “epioúsios”, a word almost unattested elsewhere.

reliquiae.note: A noun found only in the plural; from relínquere — to leave behind.

senses: release from a debt or penalty
remissio.note: A noun from remíttere — to send back, to let go; the remission of sins is the letting go of them.

repello.note: A compound of re + péllere — to push away.

resurgo.note: A compound of re- (again) + súrgere (to rise).

resurrectio.note: The noun of resúrgere, to rise again.

sabaoth.note: A Hebrew word taken into Latin unchanged and never declined; a plural, “armies” — the armies of heaven. The Vulgate translates it at Is 6:3 (“Deus exercítuum”); the liturgical books keep the Hebrew.

saeculum.note: “In sǽcula sæculórum” — a Hebrew intensifying idiom: unto the ages of ages, world without end.

salus.note: In classical Latin chiefly health and safety; in Christian Latin salvation comes to the fore.

salutare.note: The adjective salutáris (saving) used as a noun. It is the word Simeon uses of the Child in the Nunc dimíttis (Lk 2:30).

sanctifico.note: A compound of “sanctus” and “fácere” — to make holy.

sanctus.note: Often used as a noun: “Sancti”, the Saints.

scriptura.note: From scríbere (to write); in the plural Scriptúræ — the Scriptures.

secundum.note: The accusative of the adjective secúndus (following), itself from sequi (to follow) — literally “following along”.

sepelio.note: The participle sepúltus departs from the infinitive sepelíre; from the same stem comes sepultúra, burial.

spero.note: In the psalms with in and the ablative: speráre in Deo — to put one's hope in God.

senses: in the time of, under (a ruler)

tabernaculum.note: A diminutive of tabérna — a hut, a booth; in Scripture the tent of meeting.

tollo.note: In the liturgy both senses at once: the Lamb “lifts” the world's sins onto himself and so “takes them away”.

tribuo.note: Originally to share out among the tribus, the Roman tribes; hence to allot.

tristis.note: A two-termination adjective: one form for masculine and feminine (tristis), another for neuter (triste).

unigenitus.note: A compound of unus (one) + génitus (begotten) — the only one begotten.

unus.note: It takes pronominal endings in the genitive (uníus) and the dative (uni).

ut.note: With the subjunctive it means so that; with the indicative, as.

venio.note: The base of many compounds: advénio (to come to), convénio (to come together), invénio (to find).

vester.note: The possessive of the second person plural. Its form vestri also serves as the genitive of the pronoun vos.

visibilis.note: From vidére (to see); the suffix -bilis makes adjectives of possibility — able to be seen.

vita.note: The same root as vivus (alive) and vívere (to live).

vivifico.note: A compound of vivus (alive) + fácere (to make) — to make alive.

vivus.note: Used as a noun: vivi, the living.

vos.note: Its genitive has two shapes: vestri (objective, as in misereátur vestri) and vestrum (partitive).

vultus.note: Vultus is the face as it looks out — the expression; fácies is the face as a shape.
